title: Written material and diagrams
objective: See how an article and a diagram sit inside a lesson — rendered as part of the page, never in a frame.
attribution: Adapted from a note written in Crux · rendered natively here, not embedded · placeholder text

blocks.text: This is placeholder copy standing in for an article. The important thing to look at is not the words — it is that written material becomes part of this page. It uses the same typeface, the same measure, the same spacing as everything else, so nothing announces that it was authored somewhere else.

That matters because an article inside a frame brings its own fonts, its own scrollbar and its own width. The reader feels the seam immediately, and on a phone it becomes a small window inside a window.
A diagram sits inline and expands when you need it
Images are shown at the width of the reading column, which is comfortable for context but too small to study detail. Clicking opens it full screen, and Escape returns you to exactly where you were.

blocks.title: The rule this page is demonstrating
blocks.text: Anything a learner has to read becomes our own content. Anything they have to look at closely or work in can be embedded, and gets a way to fill the screen.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is an article rendered as part of the page instead of embedded in a frame?

choices.B: So it shares the same typography and width as the rest of the lesson, with no visible seam and no window-inside-a-window on mobile

checkpoint.explanation: A framed document brings its own fonts, width and scrollbar. Rendering it natively removes the seam and keeps it readable on small screens.
